title: Gene Therapy Design Principles for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
text:
Patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophin lack dystrophin expression and die of dilated
cardiomyopathy in the second or third decade of life. This proposal seeks to investigate whether
gene therapy strategies to deliver full-length dystrophin can prevent the pathogenic progression
of diseased cardiomyocytes. This innovative platform capitalizes on bioengineered hydrogels and
patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells to assess gene therapy strategies that address the
root cause of the disease.

title: Applying digital phenotypes and epigenetics to understand clinical outcomes in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure without acute respiratory distress syndrome (NAHRF)
text:
Non-acute respiratory distress syndrome acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (NAHRF) causes high morbidity
and mortality and is a major public health problem. Few effective treatments exist, at least in part due to the
syndrome’s underlying heterogeneity and the lack of appropriate target therapies. The proposed use of digital
phenotyping and epigenetics is an innovative approach to improve outcomes in NAHRF and is highly relevant
to the mission of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute to support research and training to advance
diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to predict, prevent, diagnose, and treat human diseases.

title: Determinants of immunotherapy response in NASH-Hepatocellular carcinoma
text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common type of liver cancer, is a global public health problem. The
goal of our proposal is to explore determinants of immunotherapy response in a subgroup of HCCs associated
with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) that are prone to immune evasion.

title: P30 - Core Grant for Vision Research
text:
Overall
The Core Grant for Vision Research provides support and facilities which are not available and cannot be
obtained through individual grants to 25 vision research investigators at Baylor College of Medicine, carrying
11 eligible NEI R01s. The Core facilities are used to study how visual system disorders, such as retinitis
pigmentosa, age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, amblyopia and strabismus occur and to determine
what neuronal and synaptic mechanisms in the visual system are responsible for the pathogenesis of these
disorders.

title: Center for Spillover Prevention, One Health Research, and Outbreak Readiness in Asia (SPORA)
text:
Throughout history, most widespread disease outbreaks, or pandemics, start when a pathogen is passed from
wildlife or livestock to humans. This initial spark is called a spillover and the majority of public health efforts
aimed at mitigating the impact of pandemics focus on finding these outbreaks quickly or on developing
vaccines and drugs to prevent and reduce illness and death. We propose to create a Center for Spillover
Prevention, One Health Research, and Outbreak Readiness in Asia (SPORA) with a novel pandemic mitigation
approach - to prevent pandemics before they start by stopping spillovers in the first place. We will study bats in
Bangladesh and Indonesia, because bats are the source of many new viruses, and will develop and implement
new tools to find and investigate spillovers and their root causes, leading to opportunities for prevention.

title: Gene regulatory networks controlling smooth muscle phenotype and vasculardisease risk
text:
(Public Health Relevance)
Significant expense and effort by groups of scientists around the world has identified regions of the human
genome that are associated with the genetic risk for various forms of cardiovascular disease, including
coronary artery disease. Additional research is required to understand the specific genes involved, and how
they work to contribute to the disease process. Such information will allow for better risk assessment and the
development of better therapeutics for these diseases.

title: Systems genetics of premorbid and cocaine use traits in a rat reduced complexity cross
text:
Psychostimulant use disorders, including cocaine addiction, are a major public health concern and lack FDA-
approved treatments. Despite having a known genetic component, the genetic basis of cocaine addiction is
largely unknown. This proposal seeks to use a discovery-based rodent genetic approach combined with multi-
omics analysis to rapidly identify candidate causal genes, variants, and neuroadaptive mechanisms underlying
risk traits and cocaine use traits in a highly simplified and tractable rat genetic cross.

title: Control of C. elegans Lineage by Heterochronic Genes
text:
Our focus is on antiviral defense in one of the most cost-effective genetic discovery engines in
the history of science, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, which is grown on very cheap
petri dishes and has a 3 day generation time. We generally discover 20 to 40 new genes per
year via this analysis and the genes are almost always conserved in humans. Much of the
community who work on human diseases pays attention to this C. elegans research because
so many new discoveries emerge from this research community.

title: Genetics and physiology of the tsetse fly bacterial endosymbiont Sodalis glossinidius
text:
The bacterial endosymbiont Sodalis glossinidius has been regarded as a promising paratransgenic agent for the
expression of anti-trypanosome effector molecules in tsetse flies (Glossina species). This proposal seeks to
understand the molecular basis of this symbiotic relationship by establishing how Sodalis glossinidius interacts
with insect cells and maintains a persistent infection in the tsetse host.

title: Biostatistics & Data Science Core
text: The Biostatistics and Data Science (BDS) Core will function as a central statistical and data science resource for separately funded, hypothesis-driven research studies in the Center’s areas of interest. The BDS Core will include expertise in the areas of biostatistics, led by Dr. Florin Vaida, data science, led by Dr. Benjamin Smarr, and bioinformatics and data visualization, led by Dr. Antione Chaillon. The activities of the core will be led and coordinated by Dr. Vaida. The BDS Core is mission-critical to all research projects supported by HNRC and covers a wide range of service and scientific objectives. It provides statistical expertise and resources for study design, planning, and study conduct. It provides help and expertise in analyzing data using modern statistical techniques, machine learning methods, and, more broadly, artificial intelligence (AI). It will generate novel and creative solutions to emerging data analytic questions. It will coordinate and collaborate with the NeuroAssessment, Biological Mechanisms, and Developmental Cores of HNRC, ensuring center synergy. It will train investigators in biostatistics, data science, and clinical research conduct, through seminars and individual training, consultation, and collaboration. It will perform integrative analyses for multi-omics data generated by high-throughput technological pipelines. It will ensure the scientific integrity of data analysis, and the protection of confidentiality by enforcing reproducible and ethical research principles and techniques. Special emphasis will be given to the proposed scientific aims. Building on our previous work, the Core will use machine learning methods to identify cross-sectional and longitudinal neurobehavioral phenotypes (NBP) in people with HIV (PWH). More novel will be the work of integrating biological mechanisms data into identifying brain biotypes in PWH. This task will require exploring additional AI-driven methods, for which we will engage the new members of the Core, and it will necessitate active participation from all center’s Cores. Upon completion of this research, the scientists will gain greater insights into mechanisms of interrelations between biological data and neurocognition. The use of machine learning and other proposed methods will be helpful in overcoming problems associated with analyzing high dimensional data, such as noise reduction and signal processing. Furthermore, in coordination with the other cores, the BDS Core will use statistical methods to explore the clinical relevance of identified brain biotypes. First, the biotypes themselves will be informative in that regard based on biological and clinical differences that will drive their formation. Second, the brain biotypes will be tested for association with development or progression of clinical brain health disorders, as well as medication use and self-reported behaviors. Results of this research will be informative for possible therapeutic patient-oriented interventions.

title: Ion Channels in Synaptic and Neural Circuit Physiology Course (2024-2028)
text: Fundamental advances in our understanding of the normal function of the human brain, and how this understanding can be used to combat brain disorders, will increasingly depend on researchers equipped with multidisciplinary technical expertise. This grant supports an advanced hands-on three-week summer course which provides a forum for in-depth evaluation of the emerging and converging research efforts linking ion channel biology, synaptic and circuit function to human brain physiology and disease. The course communicates fundamental concepts and cutting-edge experimental approaches to a select cadre of graduate and postgraduate trainees, who will immediately apply what they learn to their own areas of neurobiological research. This highly intensive course helps to embed the trainees in a motivated and collaborative network of like-minded scientists who are working to understand the fundamental operating principles of the central nervous system and the etiology of neurological disorders.

title: Importance of Post-translational modifications in Streptococcus mutans pathophysiology
text:
Oral infection with Streptococcus mutans strains expressing the collagen and laminin binding glycoprotein,
Cnm, is intimately associated with severe caries, systemic infections and even auto-immune disorders. We
propose to use biochemical, biophysical, genetic and microbiological approaches to characterize the Pgf post-
translational protein machinery of S. mutans. These studies are novel in Gram-positive bacteria and can
identify new targets to facilitate the development of strategies to reduce the burden not only of dental caries,
but also of diseases caused by closely related bacteria.

title: Georgia CaRes
text: A large portion of Georgia consists of rural communities that do not have adequate cancer prevention and treatment care options. The Georgia CaRes NCI Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP) aims to provide cancer prevention and control trials, cancer care delivery research (CCDR) trials, and cancer treatment trials to Georgia’s rural communities. Georgia CaRes can continue to significantly and positively impact the public health, especially with respect to cancer in rural communities in Georgia and beyond.

title: Methods for single-cell CRISPR screens and multiomic data: constructing powerful well-calibrated tests, circumventing unmeasured confounding, and accounting for denoising and imputation
text:
The number of genes that have been imputed to cause psychiatric disorders far outstrips the capacity to
study their functions. Understanding the impact of genetic risk factors would be a major step
toward improving the health and well-being of mankind. To accomplish this goal, researchers
need the right tools: our research group will develop statistical and machine learning tools to
interpret the findings of one of the most powerful tools developed in the past decade, namely
CRISPR screens.

title: Investigating the Contribution of Motor Neuronal Mitochondria to Charcot Marie Tooth Type 2D (CMT2D)
text:
Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is a collection of inherited peripheral neuropathies that affects ~1:2500
people, leading to weakness and sensory deficits in the hands and feet, and for which there is no approved
treatment. Mitochondria provide cells energy, and many of the genes mutated in CMT patients affect mitochondrial
function. Here I will combine mouse models of CMT with human cell lines engineered to carry CMT-associated
mutations to investigate the contribution of mitochondrial dysfunction to CMT2D disease etiology, potentially
identifying novel therapeutic strategies.

title: Biomarkers of Response to Immuno-chemotherapy & oliGometastatic Hypofractionated radioTherapy (BRIGHT) for Lung Cancer: Synergy of PET/CT Imaging and Peripheral Blood Assays
text:
Patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer undergo complex combinations of treatments including
chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and radiation therapy; and while some patients have prolonged cancer control
from therapy, others develop rapid progression. We propose to assess and monitor treatment response with
positron emission tomography imaging and circulating immunologic biomarkers to improve patient outcomes by
quickly detecting patients who are not benefiting from standard of care chemo-immunotherapy, and selecting for
patients whose outcomes can be improved with the addition of radiation therapy. Development and validation
of combined imaging and circulating biomarkers can support treatments that are adapted to the response of
individual patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer and improve clinical outcomes.

title: Novel role of alpha-1 antitrypsin in monocyte-driven disease activity in ANCA-associated vasculitis
text:
Morbidity and mortality in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis are due both to
disease manifestations and complications of immunosuppressive therapy. There is an urgent need for markers
of disease activity to inform management strategies that better balance benefits and risks of treatment. We
hypothesize that monocytes, key regulators of a multitude of immune responses, play an important role in
vasculitis pathogenesis, that alpha-1 antitrypsin, tied genetically to the risk of vasculitis, modulates monocyte-
driven inflammation, and that both may be valuable markers and potential targets of treatment in vasculitis.

title: A Pathomimetic Gingiva-on-a-Chip for Assessing Microbiota-Directed Anti-Inflammatory Therapeutics
text:
Periodontitis (gum disease) remains one of the most prevalent microbiome-driven inflammatory conditions
worldwide because 1) current therapies (e.g., dental cleanings) non-specifically eliminate both harmful and
beneficial oral microbes and 2) current experimental models insufficiently capture the dynamic periodontitis
disease site, hindering our ability to accurately model oral microbiome-host interactions and innovate more
targeted therapies. Recently, we discovered that a highly abundant compound in saliva, nitrate, can be converted
by beneficial microbes into an antimicrobial that selectively inhibits harmful microbes, but whether this microbe-
dependent mechanism underlies the anti-inflammatory properties of nitrate, or other unidentified compounds,
has yet to be fully explored. This project will develop a novel biomimetic platform (Gingiva-on-a-Chip) to examine
the possibility of translating nitrate, as well as novel compounds with microbe-dependent antimicrobial activity,
into more targeted anti-inflammatory therapeutics for periodontitis.

title: Novel bioinformatics methods to detect DNA and RNA modifications using Nanopore long-read sequencing
text:
We will develop efficient computational tools to detect base modifications in DNA and RNA molecules, through
analysis of ionic signals generated from the Nanopore sequencer. We will also validate these tools on cancer
samples and cell lines. These novel methods and the computational toolbox for DNA/RNA modification
detection will facilitate our understanding of the human epigenome and epitranscriptome.

title: Development Core
text: Breakthroughs in single-cell omics are providing unprecedented opportunities to investigate diverse biological questions including tissue heterogeneity, cell activity dynamics, fate determination and cellular responses to stress. Since first being described in 2009, single-cell technologies have developed rapidly, and currently most laboratories are performing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) using equipment from 10X Genomics based on droplet microfluidics. While powerful, this approach is expensive and relatively low throughput. An additional drawback to single cell technologies is that they lose spatial information due to tissue dissociation, so the physiological context cells in their niche is unknown. Understanding cellular gene expression in the context of tissue organization and morphology is critical to understanding cellular function and this is particularly true in chronic kidney disease (CKD) where injury, repair and fibrosis initiation occurs in the tubulointerstitial niche. The SCORE Core is a Resource Development Core that will address these limitations by developing and operationalizing cutting-edge technologies, and the computational pipelines required to interpret resulting data, to support the Biomedical Resource Cores and the broad kidney research community nationally. The aim of the SCORE Core is to develop new protocols and code that will illuminate the pathobiology of CKD, beginning with split pool barcoding based single nuclei multi-omics and high resolution in situ sequencing-based spatially resolved transcriptomics. We will develop protocols to employ simultaneous high-throughput ATAC and RNA expression with sequencing (SHARE-seq), a highly scalable approach for measurement of chromatin accessibility and gene expression in the same single cell, and the computational pipelines to analyze the resulting data. In addition, the SCORE Core will develop the protocols for high resolution in situ-sequencing based spatial transcriptomics using the Xenium platform. These protocols and code will be highly enabling to users in our Center, and to the Consortium broadly. The SCORE Core will also interact with the National O’Brien Consortium and Steering Committee to prioritize the development of future cutting edge technologies as they become available.
